## Small scale distribution of fish in offshore wind farms

Master thesis report in Biology

## **Kamilla Sande Hansen**

**2012**

Supervisors: Peter Rask Møller, Natural History Museum of Denmark, University of Copenhagen and Claus Stenberg, DTU Aqua.

## **Forord**

Jeg ønsker å rette en stor takk til mine veiledere, Peter Rask Møller og Claus Stenberg. Takk for deres tålmodighet, timer på feltarbeid og tid brukt for veileding og hjelp til skriveprosessen. Har satt uvurderlig stor pris dere.

Ellers ønsker jeg å takke Samsø Havvind, Vattenfall og DONG Energy for samarbeid og tilgang på deres vindmølleparker, FØNIKS som fraktet oss til Lillgrund og Middelgrund vindmøllepark og Marcus A. Krag fra Zoologisk Museum for et konstant godt humør, opplevelser Danmark rundt og hjelp til feltarbeid.

I løpet av masterperioden i Danmark har jeg mottatt stipender fra diverse selskaper og fond i Norge. Dette har gitt meg muligheten til å reise på konferanser i innland og utland, alle relevante for min utdannelse. Takk til CLIFFIMA-net, Lise & Arnfinn Hejes fond og Norges Råfisklag for økonomisk støtte.

DTU Aqua har gitt meg tilgang til alt nødvendig utstyr til både feltarbeid og skriveprosess. Tusen takk til alle gode medarbeidere og venner, både på Charlottenlund og i Hirtshals.

## **Introduction**

The aim of this thesis was to examine small-scale distribution of fish in offshore wind farms. The work is based on a literature review and a field study campaign. The thesis consists of a report and a manuscript for a scientific peer-review journal.

In the report I give an introduction to offshore wind farms as well as methods, results and discussion from my field study. In the field program I used different cameras and fishing gear methodologies in order to obtain information on fish distribution.

The part of my thesis that focuses on small scale distribution of fish (the camera methodology) is written as a manuscript for a scientific peer-review journal. I refer to this as _Paper 1_ in the text. _Paper 1_ goes through the camera methods including spatial distribution and daily variation of fish in an offshore wind farm. It also describes sampling and results of habitat classifications, and results of determination of how fish uses turbine as current shelter. _Paper 1’s_ title is _Small scale distribution of fish in offshore wind farms._

## **Background**

There is an increasing demand for energy in the world. The future lies in sustainable energy as the known non-renewable energy reserves will end at some point. Climate changes have put a focus on the need for green energy and are now a political issue. Europe is the leading continent on offshore wind power with its present capacity and will also stay in this position the upcoming years. In the end of 2011 Europe’s total offshore wind power was approximately 4 GW and with 6 GW under construction. EWEA (European Wind Energy Association) expect an increase to 40 GW offshore wind power in Europe by 2020. This will cover 4 % of Europe’s power demands (Azau & Casey, 2011).

Vindeby was the first Offshore Wind Farm (OWF) in the world and opened in Denmark in 1991. The farm has a capacity of 0.45 Mega Watts (MW) divided on 11 wind turbines and is placed 2.5 km from shore. Since 1991 about 45 OWFs has been constructed and put in operation in Europe (Azau & Casey, 2011). Denmark and United Kingdom has been among the drivers in the evolution. At present the largest OWF in operation is Thanet in UK with 300 MW divided on 100 wind turbines placed 11.3 km from shore (Thanet Offshore Wind Ltd., 2005).

Along the Danish coast there are 12 OWFs varying in size from 2 to 91 wind turbines per park in a total of 404 wind turbines (Danish Wind Turbine Owners’ Association, 2011). In 2010 Denmark had 23 % of the total offshore wind capacity in Europe (Azau & Casey, 2011) _._ When Anholt OWF opened during 2012 total offshore wind power in Denmark will be 1268 MW. This is enough to provide 1 200 000 Danish households with power from wind energy (Danish Energy Agency, 2012).

Offshore energy capacity is also increasing its share of the total energy capacity in other parts of the world. From 2009 to 2010 the offshore capacity increased from a total of 5.0 to 9.6 %.

The trend observed is larger parks in more offshore locations and at increasing water depths. Today wind farms are placed up to 100 km from shore and at 40 m water depth. OWFs at water depths up to 170 m and 200 km from shore are planned, but this demands new technology and higher efficiency (Azau & Casey, 2011). By placing OWFs far away from shore problems with local stakeholders about sound and scenery pollution is minimized (Wilson, 2007). Furthermore, the wind potential is much higher further offshore leading to higher production potential (Benassai _et al._ , 2011).

## **Wind farms effect on the local environment**

Offshore wind farms (OWF) have different kind of impacts on the environment, divided into preconstruction, construction and post-construction period with short- and/or long term effects. In preconstruction period different surveys such as seismic shooting (Wilson, 2007) and helicopter and trawl surveys (Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002). During construction there will be impacts on the environment when installing fundaments and making connections to the power grid. Long term effects are the introduction of concrete turbine, boulder and cables which have electromagnetic fields (Wilson, 2007) (Figure 1and Figure 2).

Effects on local environment are dependent on different periods. These effects can be illustrated like this:

**Figure 1: Consequences from the pre-construction/exploration and construction period of an OWF. From Elliott (2002).**

**Figure 2: Consequenses from an OWF while it operates. From Elliott (2002).**

## **Seismic shooting and acoustic surveys**

To find the appropriate locations and sediments type for the OWF, seismic shooting is performed in pre-construction period (Wilson, 2007). Seismic shooting is known to negatively affect abundance of cod ( _Gadus morhua_ (Linnaeus, 1758)) and haddock ( _Melanogrammus aeglefinus_ (Linnaeus, 1758)) (Engås _et al.,_ 1996). For lesser sandeel ( _Ammodytes marinus_ (Raitt, 1934)) a small decline in landings has been registered, but no observations of increased mortality (Hassel _et al.,_ 2004).

Acoustic mapping of the potential areas are carried out in order to show occurrence of rocky reefs, boat wrecks and bubble reef (Nicolaisen _et al.,_ 2008). This method will not affect the organisms in the area in other ways than the presence of the boat performing the measurements.

## **Sound effects/noise**

Surveys with helicopter and boats will be performed before and under the construction will be done. During construction and when the turbine runs normally and only demands maintenance, there will be ship traffic at a certain level at all times. This noise can affect the fish in the area (Petersen & Malm, 2006 and Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002).

Measurements show that the windturbines generates sounds in a large specter of Hz and the noise is spread in a large area in the OWF, both under and above sea surface (Peterson, 2001; Westerberg, 1994; Wahlberg and Westerberg 2005). Petersen & Malm (2006) mention the issue of water transmitting sound and the noise from the rotors. Noise from turbine does not have destructive effect on fish, but problems with masking communication and orientation signals can occur (Wahlberg & Westerberg, 2005).

Tougaard _et al._ (2009) showed that the harbor porpoise ( _Phocoena phocoena_ (Linnaeus, 1758)) is affected by operations driving monopile into the ground. But they reported that long term effects on the porpoise are not known as it can leave the drilling area.

## **Habitat changes**

There will be changes in habitat before, under and after construction (Petersen & Malm, 2006; Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002). Before construction core drilling is done to get an overview over sediment layers in the OWF area _._ Seabed will change in the period when cable route is made, either by trenching or tunneling. This increases turbidity and is considered a short-term effect (Wilson, 2007). There will also be changes when placing the wind turbine fundament on ground but the placing itself is considered a short-term effect. These two actions can affect some benthic species (Jensen _et al.,_ 2003) but the species are believed to return to the OWF again when the construction period is over (Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002).

Boulders are placed around each turbine to prevent erosion of sediment (den Boon _et al.,_ 2004).The boulder will also create a change in habitat as rocks are introduced in the area. It will also decrease the natural habitat, often sandy seabed. Boulder creates and functions as an artificial rock reef or fish aggregation device (FAD) (Pickering _et al.,_ 1999 and Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006). Long term effects are physical changes, as the introduction of concrete fundaments and boulders and subsequent changes in currents in the farm (Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002). A wind turbine can be viewed as an artificial reef as it cuts through the water column and are being placed at the seabed (Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006). Artificial reefs are known to increase fish diversity in the vicinity of the reef substrate (Pickering _et al.,_ 1999 and Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006).

The position of OWF on relatively shallow water with introduction of increased habitat complexity (turbine constructions and boulders) makes the OWF a potential nursery for a range of marine mammals, fish and crustaceans (Cléirigh, 2000; Foreward, 2005; Linley _et al.,_ 2007).

## **Co-use and function of OWF**

It has been suggested that OWF can be used for aquaculture or farming, mussel aquaculture (Buck, 2006, 2007; Michler-Cieluch _et al.,_ 2009) and lobsters ranching (Cléirigh, 2000) have been proposed as good candidates. Especially the ranching concept seems to be ideal for lobsters or other stationary species which can be released as fry or juveniles in the area and will have good chances of remaining in the area due to the boulder habitat around the turbines. Furthermore, fishing is usually prohibited in an OWF (van Deurs _et al.,_ accepted). This makes them the facto marine protected areas (MPA) even though it has been questioned whether they will function as such for fish due to their relatively small spatial area in comparison to that utilized in the life cycle (Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011).

## **Step stones**

Surrounding habitat of an OWF is assumed to have some influence on the species diversity in the area. With a natural rock reef in close distance it is believed that the diversity and amount of fish in area already is quite large. Species preferring hard substrate, such as epi-benthic fauna, will easier, quicker and in a larger amount use the boulder in an OWF as new habitat and use it as a stepping stone for further distribution (Petersen & Malm 2006; Perkol-Finkel & Benayahi 2006). PerkolFinkel and Benayahi (2006) showed in their study from the Red Sea that organisms colonize and that new reef is adding, and not detracting, species from surrounding reefs and areas. To what degree and speed the re-colonization will be affected depends on the amount of damages made when creating the park (Petersen & Malm, 2006). It is also a matter for how long the park has been up and running as the fauna is influenced by the activity during the building of the OWF (Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002).

## **Electromagnetic fields**

Whether cables can create long-terms effect by electromagnetic fields has been discussed in the literature (Meiβner & Sordyl, 2006; Öhman _et al.,_ 2007). There are cables within the OWF as well as cables from the farm transporting electricity to the power grid at shore. Cables used for electric transmission in the sea have an influence on some fish species using geomagnetic field for orientation and the magnetic fields can affect the migration and stationary fish in the area (Öhman _et al.,_ 2007; Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002). This includes both bony fishes and elasmobranch fishes. Elasmobranchs have the ampullae of Lorenzini which is considered to be the organ which perceives

the electrical signal (Kalmijn, 1982) and it is therefore believed that elsamobranchs will be affected by the elctromagnetic cables. Some species of bony fishes are shown to be magneto sensitive because of magnetic materials (Fe) in the lagenal otolith (Harada _et al._ , 2001; Öhman _et al.,_ 2007).

## **Hydrological conditions**

Hydrological conditions such as changes in current strength might occur in an OWF (Jensen _et al.,_ 2003; Hoffmann _et al.,_ 2002). This is still a discussed theme as the OWFs of today might not be large enough to have significant impact on large scale current. However, at the local level the piles and turbine construction is known to affect the local current regime (Johansen _et al.,_ 2008; Stenberg _et al.,_ 2010).

## **Field survey**

Data sampling to this study was from fieldwork done in the Øresund Strait during summer/fall 2011 using different sampling methods and equipment. There is already some research done on OWFs in large scale and will be mentioned and discussed as background for the hypotheses (e.g. Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011; Couperus, 2010; Bergström _et al.,_ 2009).

The purpose with this project was to analyze the small scale distribution of fish in an OWF. Hypothesis was that turbines and boulder around the turbine will function as an artificial reef and thereby increase fish abundance. Some of OWFs have a fishery prohibition (van Deurs _et al., accepted)_ mainly with gear as bottom trawl in order to protect power cables. Boulder combined with fishing prohibition  is believed to provide an small scale marine protected area (MPA) for some species (Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011; Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006).

Knowledge about small scale distribution of fish around turbines in an OWF thus remains relatively scarce as it is difficult to monitor with acoustic gear and traditional fishing gears (fish fyke, gillnets, trawl, etc.). Until now research done in OWFs to determine small scale distribution of fish is mainly done by acoustic methods (Couperus _et al.,_ 2010) or scuba diver (Öhman & Wilhelmsson, 2005; Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006). Studies and observations show indications that in an OWF the turbines function as an aggregation point for fish (e.g. Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006; Couperus _et al.,_ 2010). However, the equipment is expensive and to prevent damages it is not placed very close to the turbine (Couperus _et al.,_ 2010). Acoustic measurements done in Couperus _et al._ (2010) and sampling with gillnets as in Leonhard _et al._ (2011) do not provide enough detailed information about small scale distribution of fish in an OWF or how the fish is distributed in the immediate vicinity of the turbine.

It is hypothesized that the fish uses the turbines as an aggregation point in lack of shelter or preferable substrate in the area and that the OWF will increase the fish abundance. A method using underwater video (StatCam) to qualify and quantify fish distribution and utilization of a small area was therefore developed. The advantage with these methods compared to acoustic measurements is the absence of a boat which potentially can scare fish while in the OWF. StatCam also has the advantage that it can be left in the sea for days filming at the exact same spot. The method with all its specifications is found in _Paper 1._

It is also believed that the fish will use the turbine as a shelter or protection from the currents. By using the turbine the fish can still feed in the water column when strong current and do not have to seek the seabed for shelter.

Increased knowledge in small scale distribution and how the fish uses the turbine as a shelter can be used for the purpose of co-use or multi functions of an OWF and to understand if the farm can function as a marine protected area (MPA) or to get a deeper insight in the species composition in an OWF.

Two different OWFs were investigated during the project. Lillgrund OWF is placed east of Malmø in Swedish waters and Middelgrund is placed north of Lillgrund in Danish waters. Both OWF are placed in the Øresund Strait (Figure 3).

## **Sites**

Sites were chosen on the background of different physical conditions. The original plan was to sample data in Frederikshavn, Samsø and Horns Reef I OWF. These sites have a difference in depth, salinity (Figure 3), and sediment (Figure 4). Due to technical issues with the cameras and as a results lack of time, the sites used for present the study focus on results from Middelgrund and Lillgrund, both located in the Øresund Strait.

Lillgrund and Middelgrund turbines have gravity based fundament (GBS). GBS has either a circular, conical or square shaped concrete fundament placed on the seabed and filled up with gravel to increase weight (Azau & Casey, 2011; Wilson, 2007). GBS are used in waters with depth up to 30 m (Azau & Casey, 2011).

## **Frederikshavn**

Frederikshavn OWF was established in 2003 with three turbines with a total of 7 MW (Figure 3). The park is mainly for development and demonstration of new wind turbines (Danish Energy Agency, 2012).  The farm was visited 16[th] to 18[th] of May 2011. One gillnet was set but caught only nine fish in total. StatCam were tested in the sea for the first time but due to technical problems and harsh weather the trip to Frederikshavn gave no results. Our snorkeler did not observe any fish at the wind turbine.

## **Horns Reef I**

Horns Reef I is placed 14 to 20 km off Denmark’s west coast in the North Sea. With its 80 wind turbines and 160 MW it produces enough energy for 150 000 Danish households (DONG Energy _et al.,_ (2006) and have a squared shape.

Horns Reef I was never visited due to technical problems with StatCam.

## **Samsø**

There are ten windmills with a total of 23 MW placed at _Paludans Flak I/S_ 3.5 km south of Samsø (Figure 3) (Jørgensen _et al.,_ 2007; Danish Energy Agency, 2012). Only one of the StatCams was placed in the sea due to technical problems with the other two. But as a result of really harsh weather the visibility in sea was poor and trip to Samsø gave no results. Data sampling at Samsø was performed 23[rd] to 24[th] of May 2011.

Lillgrund OWF was opened in 2008. It consists of 48 turbines with gravity based fundament and is placed 7 km west of Malmø at the Swedish coastline (Figure 3). The OWF is placed on depth from 4 to 8 m (Jeppsson _et al._ , 2008).

Lillgrund was visited twice for different data sampling. First in mid-October with StatCam and CTD probe, then again in November to sample data about how fish uses the turbine as shelter for currents.

Middelgrund OWF was opened in 2001 with 20 turbines each of 2 MW (Petersen, 2004).  The farm is placed in a curved line pointing north-south. As an old waste dumping area for the Copenhagen area, Middelgrund is shallower (2 to 6 m) than the surrounding areas (Middelgrunden Wind Turbine Cooperative).

Since all the turbines are placed on a line the current changes will most likely not be big. The boulder used in the OWF is not visible above the seabed as sand has covered it all during the 11 years it has been running.

## **Method**

In order to obtain detailed information on the environmental characteristics of the areas and to be able to test the hypothesis mentioned above, a suite of sampling methods and gears were used.

Seabed surveys were made to get information about sediments and benthic/sessile organisms creating the habitat for fish in the areas. StatCam was developed for this project to show how the small scale distribution of fish is in an OWF and how the fish uses the turbines as an aggregation point in lack of shelter or preferable substrate in the area.

To be able to determine how the fish uses the turbines as current shelter four cameras were set as close as possible to the turbine, two in the zone with shelter from the currents and two in the zone with current.

Gillnets and –traps were used to create a data base of fish species in the area at Middelgrund. At Lillgrund a solid data base for fish species present in the area already existed (Bergström _et al.,_ 2009).

## **Cameras**

Different camera methods were developed for this project. StatCam which is a stationary camera placed on the sea bed and turbine camera used for to close-up video of the turbine and surrounding areas.  Acoustic measurements done in Couperus _et al._ (2010) do not provide enough of information about small scale distribution of the fish in the OWF.

## **StatCam**

In this project the StatCam was used to sample information on fish distribution at and around selected turbines in two OWF in order to examine how the fish uses the turbines as an aggregation point in lack of shelter or preferable substrate in the area. A detailed description of the methods is described in _Paper 1_ .

**Figure 5: Installation of StatCam with camera installed on pile on seabed and cylinder in surface containing battery and recorder. Camera point in direction of turbine.**

StatCam was installed on a heavy concrete pile with opportunity to regulate weight from 15 to 25 kg to keep the camera as stable as possible. An anchor between camera and recorder/battery pack created stability for the camera as well; it prevented the battery pack in the surface to drag the StatCam around on the sea bed. From the metal stand in the pile there was a floating buoy in the surface. The buoy was deflated to prevent the waves to drag it along and tip the camera but could still be used to lower and raise camera.

The battery pack was developed a lot during the study. When floating in the surface there is a heavy impact on the technical equipment. The last version of the battery pack included a recorder glued to a plate and wires taped to keep them stable.

Recorded data was analyzed in Windows Media Player. The screen was divided into 9 to 72 squares to facilitate the counting. Fish that was observed between squares was counted to the left and up to avoid double counting:

**Figure 6: When counting fish recorded a grid system were placed over the computer screen to avoid re-counting. When a fish were placed under one of the lines in the grid system they were counted in the square either to the left or up.**

## **TurbCam**

To be able to determine how the fish uses the turbines as current shelter four small cameras where each was mounted on a metal stand 1.5 m above sea bed (Figure 7). A detailed description of the method is found in _Paper 1_ .

Records from camera at the turbines were analyzed by counting the amount of fish in different zones. The camera has a 360 degree angle to film in which gave a 4 × 90 degrees zone division. These divisions were named after placing in relation to the current. Zones in current was named CU followed by a letter, a-d. And the zones in the wind turbines current shelter were named SH followed by a letter, a-d. The letter _d_ is always the area closest to the fundament (see _Paper 1_ ). During the data processing it was realized that the grouping into _a, b_ and _c_ were too detailed and consequent the reported data in _Paper 1_ also whether the fish was in the shelter or exposed site of the turbine.

**Figure 7: Installation of Turbine Camera. Arrow indicates camera. The square is the steering plate to keep the camera stable.**

## **Transects**

Habitat types at was classified according to sediment type and associated sessile flora and fauna. For details see _Paper 1_ .

## **Fish sampling techniques**

Fish species present in the OWF area were examined by gillnets, fish fykes and visual by snorkelers. Besides providing a suite of sampling methods that could be compared, the data was used to help identify specimens seen on film (StatCam).

At Lillgrund there is already a solid data base for fish species present in the area.  Database for species in Lillgrund OWF is found in a control program from Lillgrund and can be seen in Appendix as Table 4. Gear used for the sampling was gillnets and fish fykes (Bergström _et al.,_ 2009).

At Middelgrund data were sampled by using gillnets and fish fykes and observations from a snorkeler. Data from Danish Fish Atlas (www.fiskeatlas.dk) were combined with the data from the fish gear (Appendix Table 5). Registrations in Danish Fish Atlas are from the area around and in Middelgrund OWF where species are registered by snorkeler caught in fish fyke or gillnet.

## **Gillnets**

Nets used for sampling are multi-mesh gillnets called coastal- and fjord net (Eigaard _et al.,_ 2000). These were developed by Danish Institute for Fisheries and Research (DIFRES) (Støttrup _et al.,_ 2003).  Net were 1.5 m tall and mounted on a buoyancy line and a lead line. Total length of net was 100 m with one meter between each panel. Mesh size used varied from 6.5 to 116.7 mm half-mesh (Table 3). Panels with mesh size up to 14.3 mm had a length of three meters, panel with mesh size from 18.6 to 40.9 mm had a length of six meters and panels with mesh size from 53.1 to 116.7 mm length was 12 m.

The net was deployed in the afternoon and retrieved following morning. At deployment the depth range was recorded. Total fishing time was thus around 18 hours from 1700 hours in the afternoon to 10 a.m. After retrieval the net was taken to port and the fish was identified to species, length measured and weighted.

With small mesh sizes the threads used is very thin. This creates a net that will easily collapse with strong currents. To avoid this net were always placed in same direction as the current.

## **Fish fyke**

Three fish fykes were placed at different distances to the turbine. The fyke was 65 cm tall with a lead line and a buoyancy line with total of six meters and had a half mesh size of 8 mm. Fish fykes are placed at the seabed catching mainly benthic and benthopelagic species.

The fykes were deployed around 1500 hours and retrieved at the same time the following day. They were emptied while in the OWF which gave the opportunity of having the fykes in the sea in a 24 hours cycle only obstructed by a 40 minutes period while retrieving and deploying gear.

**Figure 9: Illustration of a half fish fyke, it is similar in both ends. Fish swim into the panel and are led into the cage on either left or right.**

## **Snorkeler**

At Middelgrund a snorkeler was observing fish species and distribution. By snorkeling in the area around the turbine and StatCam species were observed and registered in fish fykes and in the water column. Placing of StatCam was also easier as the snorkeler easily placed them with correct angle and direction.

## **Physical data**

Temperature and salinity measurements were done on a daily basis using WTW COND 240i with a TetraCan 325 probe. Water was collected with water sampler temperature from the seabed. Water for salinity measurements were collected from the surface.

## **CTD**

Physical data on salinity, temperature and oxygen was sampled by a Seabird SBE9 CTD (Conductivity, Temperature and Depth). Sampling was performed along an East-West transect in Lillgrund and Middelgrund OWF. The CTD probe was lowered at around 0.5 m/sec from surface to bottom. Sampling was performed along a transect perpendicular to the OWF from shallow to deep waters.

Analysis of data was done in the software Surfer 9 using the procedure kriging with the settings “Linear” with a 1.25 ratio.

## **Current**

The currents in the area of both Lillgrund and Middelgrund were collected from Danish Maritime Safety Administration (http://ifm.frv.dk/). Information is registered at Drogden light house, south of Copenhagen. Placed between the two OWFs and data is believed to be representative for both farms (Figure 3).

## **Results**

## **Habitat classifications**

Results from Habitat classification with its graphs and results can be seen in _Paper 1_ . As summary, we found large differences in seabed habitat and species compositions. Lillgrund has sandy seabed with large coverage of _Mytilus._ While at Middelgrund boulders and pebbles covers much of transects. Distribution of _Zostera_ and macro algae (dominated by red algae) was larger in Middelgrund than for Lillgrund.

## **Analysis of movies from StatCam**

Results from StatCam with its graphs and results can be seen in _Paper 1_ . In summary, we found that the fish abundance was highest at the stations zero meters from the turbines in both Lillgrund and Middelgrund OWF, compared to the two other stations at 25 and 50 m away. However, while the difference in fish abundance in Lillgrund was statistical significant and a factor 100 higher close to the turbine compared to the two other stations, the difference at Middelgrund was only a factor 1.5 and not statistical significant. Two-spotted goby ( _Gobiusculus flavescens_ (Fabricius, 1779)) was the species observed the most at StatCam and by diver/snorkeler for both Lillgrund and Middelgrund.

## **Turbine studies**

Results can be seen in _Paper 1_ . In summary we found that at low current velocity less than 40 cm/s the fish does not show indications on leaving the turbine to seek areas with less current. From the film it is seen that the fish uses the turbine actively and is approximately 1 to 5 cm from the concrete when in the _Current_ side of the turbine. But as the speed differences in this study are so low (35 to 47 m/s) it is hard to draw a conclusion on how the fish uses the turbine for currentshelter.

## **Analysis of fish caught from gillnets and fish fykes**

Catches differed in size and species composition dependent on fish gear used. Fish gear was just used at Middelgrund since Bergström _et al._ (2009) have made a data base for Lillgrund (Table 4).

A total of 38 species is registered in the area in and around Middelgrund by Danish Fish Atlas surveys and through this study. At Lillgrund 14 species is registered (Table 4) (Bergström _et al.,_ 2009).

An overview of fish registered at Lillgrund is placed in Appendix (Table 4). These registrations are done in a control program for the Swedish Agency for Marine and Water Management. For results from StatCam see _Paper 1._

Gear, fish species, weight and length per individual were registered. In total 15 species were registered in the two fish gears with goldsinny wrasse ( _Ctenolabrus rupestris_ (Linnaeus, 1758)) and three-spined stickleback ( _Gasterosteus aculeatus_ (Linnaeus, 1758)) as dominating species from gillnet. For fish fyke cod were the dominating species.

No two-spotted goby were caught in gillnet, but four were caught in fish fyke, 500 registered by snorkeler and 29 191 registered at StatCam (Figure 13). Four perch ( _Perca fluviatilis_ (Linnaeus, 1758)) were registered in gillnet, but were not registered by any other method. Gillnet and fish fyke shows big diversity in fish species. The most numerous species caught with gillnet was goldsinny wrasse, three-spined stickleback and cod ( _G. morhua_ ). For fish fyke cod _(Gadu morhua_ (Linnaeus, 1758)), perch ( _P. fluviatilis_ ) and viviparous eelpout ( _Zoarces viviparous_ (Linnaeus, 1758)) was the most numerous species. Viviparous eelpout ( _Z. viviparus_ ), two-spottet goby ( _G.  flavescens_ , sand goby ( _Pomatoschistus minutus_ (Pallas, 1770)) and eel ( _A. anguilla)_ were all caught in the fyke but not in any other gear.

For full species list from Middelgrund see Appendix Table 5. For results from StatCam see _Paper 1._

## **Physical data**

Øresund area has a mix of salinity in the water column. The upper layer is determined by the runoff from the Baltic Sea. This water has low salinity and weighs less than the water coming in from the North-Sea. With two different salinities there a halocline is created in the water column. This will fluctuate during season depending on the amount of run-off from the Baltic Sea and amount of water from the North-Sea.

Water with higher salinity pushes in through Øresund Strait and gives the high salinity water close to seabed. Lillgrund has a heterogonous water column with temperature that differs in transect. Water from the Baltic Sea is fresher and with a lower temperature than the salter water west in transect.  At Middelgrund a homogenous water column was observed.

In Middelgrund OWF average salinity was 7.55 ‰ in August, for September it was 11.32 ‰ and in Lillgrund OWF salinity was 8.85 ‰ in October.

## **Discussion**

When introducing turbines and boulders to an area the natural habitat changes and as a result of this species occurrence and distribution is believed to change as well. It is well known that many species of fish gather around both natural hard substrates such as reefs and rocks as well as near artificial structures such as bridges, platforms, wrecks and OWFs (Castro _et al.,_ 2002; Soldal _et al.,_ 2002; Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006). Several studies have focused on this issue (e.g. Andersson & Öhman, 2010; Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006), but detailed studies of the small scale distribution of fish in OWFs are still missing (Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011). _Paper 1_ shows that various camera systems have a great potential for the study of small scale distribution of fish in OWFs.

By using different fish gears in this study a diversion in species composition and in number of fish caught per fish gear is shown. Present study shows the need for more than one method to understand the composition of fish species in an area.  This has also been showed in earlier studies (e.g. Dearden _et al.,_ 2010; Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011; Soldal _et al.,_ 2002). Different methods give indications of the distribution of fish and fish species in the OWF on a larger scale than StatCam were able to show.  While some species are active at night others are absent in the same period. Gillnets and fish fykes catch fish also during night, while the camera recorded during daytime and therefore only get results from day active species.

Observations done around turbine to see how fish uses turbine as shelter for currents show that fish aggregate around the turbine at currents lower than 40 cm/s. But as the speed differences in this study was small (35 to 47 m/s) it is hard to draw a conclusion on how the fish uses the turbine for current-shelter.

The advantage of the camera methods compared to diver/snorkeler is the possibility to sample information on fish distribution and behavior on a high spatial scale without any interruption as a diver can cause (Dearden _et al.,_ 2010). Stationary gear as fish fyke and gillnet does not demand for presence of a boat, potentially scaring the fish for a long period. Other types of large physical sampling gears (e.g. trawl or acoustical gear at a boat) that visually or by noise can potentially scare fish and bias sampling results.  On the other hand camera has the disadvantages of sampling over a relatively narrow spatial scale compared to the other sampling methods mentioned above, and are dependent on good visibility and day-light conditions to function and thereby mainly be operational at relatively shallow depth (due to light conditions).

Hydro acoustic methods were used to determine large and small scale distribution of fish at Horn Reef I and Nysted OWF (DONG Energy _et al.,_ 2006). When using acoustic measurements no proof of turbine functioning as aggregation point was achieved in Horns Reef I. While at Nysted an increase in epi-benthic community was found, but no indications for increased fish abundance (DONG Energy _et al.,_ 2006). At Horns Reef I, increased species diversity among reef-fish around the turbine was registered when using gillnets (Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011). Surveys done with trawl and sonar scans around oil platforms have not been able to determine distribution < 50 m from rig (Soldal _et al.,_ 2002). Soldal _et al._ (2002) showed spatial distribution with installing acoustic transducers close to the platform.

Placing five nets of 100 m in length and 1.5 m in height gave a much bigger coverage area than StatCam. Each net fished for approximately 18 hours from 1700 hours in the afternoon to 10 a.m. While the StatCam gave information from a maximum of 11 hours, from 8 a.m. to sunset or memory card was full. Information from gillnets gives information about fish distribution in a larger scale than StatCam. Results from gillnets provide information of which species we can expect to see on the film and how the fish was distributed in a larger scale in the OWF. A gillnet covers an area of approximately 100 m, a fish fyke 30 m and the StatCam an area of maximum 5 m along the seabed and up in the water column. Gillnets and fish fykes have the possibility of fishing for a longer period per day that StatCam since the camera not will be able to record due to bad light conditions more than one hour before sunrise and one hour after sunset. This creates a difference in what species caught and filmed. The area coverage and the time difference create different results.

It was the same gillnets used for this study as for Horns Reef I studies as used for this study at Middelgrund. At Horns Reef I nets were set in directions with currents from ~0 m, ~120 m and ~230 m from turbine (Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011). Indications from the reports’ results show that the nets do not provide data on a small enough scale to determine fish distribution close to turbine (< 50 m). Sampling for present study performed at Middelgrund, only four two-spotted gobies were caught with fish fyke, but the StatCam and turbine studies still show a high abundance. Sampling was not done with gillnets or fish fykes at Lillgrund as Bergström _et al.,_ (2009) have made a species list from the area.

As observed in this and other studies (e.g. Andersson & Öhman, 2010; Wilhelmsson _et al.,_ 2006) two-spotted goby is the most abundant species around the turbines, where they feed on planktonic copepods (Costello _et al.,_ 1990; Nicolajsen _et al.,_ 1983). With its large dark spot placed at the

peduncle, often saddles on the back two-spotted gobies are usually easy to recognize (Bracken & Kennedy, 1967). It is believed that the turbulence created around the turbine will enhance access to copepods in the whole water column. Andersson & Öhman (2010) observed juveniles, adults and gravid females around the turbines. Mussels and macro algae surrounding the turbine provide twospotted gobies with nests. Spawning takes place in March to August on depth < 5 m (Skolbekken & Utne-Palm, 2001). Based on depth, both Lillgrund and Middelgrund should be good as spawning areas. At Lillgrund, the boulder around the turbines is placed approximately 0.5-1 m above seabed which makes the turbines good spawning places despite the deeper surrounding areas. At Lillgrund, the boulder are completely covered in mussels which the two-spotted goby can use as nest for their eggs, which is guarded by the male (Skolbekken & Utne-Palm, 2001). Cod fish are known to be one of the main predators on two-spotted gobies (Fosså, 1991).

## **Conclusion**

Discussion around spatial distribution, daily variation of fish, habitat classifications and how fish uses turbine as shelter can be seen in _Paper 1_ . As a summary it can be mentioned that areas with homogeneous sand sediment has a higher impact on the fish fauna compared to OWF in areas with heterogonous sediment. The study found that the fish fauna near the wind turbines was dominated by two-spotted gobies, ( _G. flavescens_ ) with a significant difference in numbers for Lillgrund and Middelgrund OWF.  This suggests that the vertical structure of the wind turbine through the water column function as a fish aggregation point, dependent on the surrounding habitat. The hypothesis of fish using turbine as shelter for current cannot be confirmed or disproved with achieved results. Furthermore, the effect of OWF on fish appears to be on a much smaller scale than previously thought.

Information from this thesis can later be used for the understanding if an OWF can function as a marine protected area. Also for the development of co-use of an OWF for the purpose of breeding species such as fish or crustaceans this can be useful information.

## **Further development of this method**

The restricting part in this study has been the technical issues. The StatCam should be able to record in HD-quality, not in 720 × 480 as used here. This would make it easier to identify the different species. By adding an external hard-disc in the black cylinder it would be possible to leave the cameras at sea without handling the equipment. It would be ideal to place the StatCam in the sea and leave it recording for a week.

It would be a benefit to film during night in order to register nocturnal species. An option could be infrared but as the red light get absorbed fast it might be better with photographs taken with flash. This will probably scare the fish from the area for a given time but will give some indications on the activity in the area.

By using StatCam over a longer period of time, seasons and yearly changes can be studied. In areas where OWF are planned the StatCam can be used for the pre-construction surveys. Later it can be used to compare the before and after impacts on the area.

StatCam has already been tested in monitoring of mussel banks, and has been used for seeking after gear lost at sea. Similar methods as used here with StatCam has earlier been used for monitoring coral reefs (Dearden _et al.,_ 2010)

This method could possibly also be used to monitor cable routes to identify how species react differently to electromagnetic cables.

## Paper 1: Small scale distribution of fish in offshore wind farms

Article draft

**Kamilla Sande Hansen 01-01-2012**

Co-authors: Claus Stenberg, DTU Aqua and Peter Rask Møller,  Natural History Museum of Denmark, University of Copenhagen

## **Abstract**

A stationary camera system was used to study the small scale distribution of fish in the two offshore wind farms (OWF) Middelgrund and Lillgrund in Øresund Strait, between Denmark and Sweden. Fish distribution was examined at approximately 0, 25 and 50 m from the turbines. The study found that the fish fauna near the wind turbines was dominated by two-spotted gobies, _Gobiusculus flavescens_ (Fabricius, 1779). There was a significant difference in numbers of fish for Lillgrund and Middelgrund OWF. At Lillgrund sediment was dominated of bare sand while Middelgrund had more heterogeneous sediment types with sand, boulder, pebbles and dense eelgrass areas. This suggests that OWF in areas with homogeneous sand sediment has a higher impact on the fish fauna compared to OWF in areas with heterogonous sediment. Furthermore, the effect of OWF on fish appears to be on a much smaller scale than previously thought.

## **Introduction**

Offshore wind farms (OWF) is increasing in the world, with Europe as a leading continent (Azau & Casey, 2011). OWF’s have until know been placed in relatively shallow waters (< 20 m) and on sandy seafloor habitats due to engineering constrains and to minimize establishment cost. Establishment of an OWF introduces a new habitat type with turbine construction and erosion protections by boulders to the sandy habitat (Petersen & Malm, 2006). Introduced hard substrate by boulders, turbine foundation on seabed and the vertical part of the turbine that cuts through water column has the potential to effect the marine environment. Hard substrate provides a new habitat for species associated to this habitat type and a subsequent habitat loss for species associated to sand habitat. Perkol-Finkel & Benayahi (2006) showed that organisms colonizing a new reef are adding, and not detracting, species from surrounding reefs and areas. Added hard substrate can be viewed as an artificial reef (e.g. Wilhelmsson _et al_ ., 2006a). Wilhelmsson _et al._ (2006a) showed that species such as blue mussels and red algae occurred in higher density around the turbine than elsewhere in the OWF-area.

Studies in in OWFs on fish have mainly been done by gillnets, trawls (Klaustrup, 2006, Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011), sledge (van Deurs, _accepted_ ), hydro acoustic methods (Leonhard _et al.,_ 2011; Couperus _et al.,_ 2010) or divers (Öhman & Wilhelmsson, 2005; Andersson & Öhman, 2010). None of these studies have shown any overall negative effects on fish abundance or diversity in an OWF. Several studies indicate that fish aggregates around turbines at a small

scale (e.g. Santos _et al._ 1996; Wilhelmsson _et al_ ., 2006a).  However, the methods used have not allowed a high spatial resolution or been able to obtain data from very close to the turbines or boulder protection. Therefore, knowledge about small scale distribution of fish around turbines in offshore wind farms has remained relatively scarce.

A method using underwater video (StatCam) to qualify and quantify fish distribution and utilization with high spatial resolution around wind turbines was therefore developed. Advantage with these methods compared to sonar scans is the absence of a boat which potentially can scare fish while in the wind farm area. The method with underwater video have been used with success monitoring coral reef fish (Dearden _et al.,_ 2010), but to our knowledge it has not been used before for monitoring in OWFs.

StatCam give pictures of spatial fish distribution in an OWF and information on how the fish is distributed during the day. These distributions patterns vary dependent on the habitat present in the different OWFs. As for Lillgrund the OWF gave an introduction of boulders in an area mostly consisting of sandy seabed. While for Middelgrund boulders were already present and the introduction of the boulder around the turbine is not believed to have the same impact on the habitat changes.

Increased knowledge in small scale distribution and how the fish uses the turbine as a shelter can be used for the purpose of co-use or multi functions of an OWF and to understand if the farm can function as a marine protected area (MPA) or to get a deeper insight in the species composition in an OWF.

The aim to present in this project was to analyze the small scale distribution of fish in an OWF. It is hypothesized that the fish uses the turbines as an aggregation point in lack of shelter or preferable substrate in the area and that the OWF will increase the fish abundance. It is also believed that the fish will use the turbine as a shelter or protection from the currents to save energy. Another theory is that fish uses the turbine to easy access to food by feeding on the growth on the turbine itself or by feeding vertical in water column. Regarding variation during day it is hypothesized that occurrence of small fish will dominate during day while larger fish and predators are expected to enter the farm when sun sets.
